WaterKron and FlipFlop Hessian: Information-Theoretically Grounded Quantization with Kronecker-factored Hessians

Johann Birnick & Rayan Saab Affiliation: Department of Mathematics Affiliation: University of California San Diego Affiliation: La Jolla, CA 92093, USA Email: {jbirnick,rsaab}@ucsd.edu
Abstract

How should a Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation be chosen for post-training quantization? We address this question through WaterKron, which combines two-sided GPTQ with row- and column-dependent waterfilling scales and entropy coding. We derive its high-rate distortion with respect to the full Hessian using an explicit Kronecker-Hessian mismatch factor Φ\Phi. This factor quantifies the asymptotic distortion penalty due to the Kronecker Hessian approximation and provides a criterion for selecting the factors optimally. Minimizing Φ\Phi leads to a Gaussian covariance-fitting problem with classical “flip-flop” updates. We thus give a rate-distortion justification for using the resulting FlipFlop Hessian in quantization. We evaluate it empirically, finding that the FlipFlop Hessian consistently improves KL divergence and perplexity over input-only, marginal, and Frobenius-based Hessian choices.

1 Introduction

Post-training quantization of neural networks is the process of taking a fully trained neural network, and converting its high-precision weights into a low-precision format, with the goal of retaining accuracy while reducing memory requirements. Usually, each linear module WW is quantized separately. Hence the goal is to find a low-precision approximation VV of WW.

There exist different classes of algorithms for finding such a VV, which can also be combined. Some methods focus on making the entries of WW incoherent and thus easier to quantize, for example by utilizing random or learned rotations (Chee et al., 2023; Ashkboos et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Other methods change the base quantizer that is applied to a single or small group of entries, for example by using codebooks or lattices instead of simple rounding (Tseng et al., 2024a; Savkin et al., 2025). A third class of methods does “adaptive rounding” by conditioning the quantization of later entries within WW such that they correct the errors introduced by quantizing earlier entries of WW.

Our work falls within the realm of this third class of methods, more concretely into its largest subclass that might be labeled “error propagation under a quadratic loss”.

A prominent example within this line of research is the GPTQ algorithm by Frantar et al. (2023). In order to measure the distortion when WW is replaced by VV, the algorithm uses a quadratic loss. However, instead of just looking at ∥V−W∥F\lVert V-W\rVert_{F}, for which simple “round to nearest” is the optimal quantization algorithm, it takes into account the input x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} of the linear module WW, and measures the distortion as 𝔼​∥V​x−W​x∥22\mathbb{E}\lVert Vx-Wx\rVert_{2}^{2}. In practice, the expectation is taken over a calibration dataset.

This algorithm has been analyzed and extended from different directions (Chee et al., 2023; Tseng et al., 2024a; Tseng et al., 2024b; Zhang et al., 2026; Tseng et al., 2026; Birnick, 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025; Ordentlich and Polyanskiy, 2026; Lifar et al., 2026, e.g.,), but central for this paper are the following two improvements:

  1. 1.

    The extension to a two-sided geometry, as described by Kim et al. (2025); Tseng et al. (2026); Birnick and Saab (2026). In standard GPTQ, the rows of W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} are treated all equally, in a batched way. Formally, when we vectorize the matrices of interest into w=vec⁡(W)∈ℝm​nw=\vecop(W)\in\mathbb{R}^{mn} and v=vec⁡(V)v=\vecop(V), then the Hessian of the loss 𝔼​∥(V−W)​x∥22\mathbb{E}\lVert(V-W)x\rVert_{2}^{2} with respect to vv is 2​𝔼​[x​xT]⊗Im2\mathbb{E}[xx^{T}]\otimes I_{m}. While the 𝔼⁡[x​xT]\mathbb{E}[xx^{T}] factor corresponds to the input geometry that GPTQ exploits, the identity factor ImI_{m} means that all output features are treated equally. There is a natural extension of GPTQ that can deal with arbitrary Kronecker-factored Hessians A⊗BA\otimes B, and reduces to standard GPTQ if B=ImB=I_{m}. This variant of the algorithm effectively minimizes the loss ∥(B1/2)T​(V−W)​A1/2∥F2\lVert(B^{1/2})^{T}(V-W)A^{1/2}\rVert_{F}^{2}, in particular the factor BB in the Hessian also informs the algorithm of the output geometry of the linear module WW. For the exact choice of the Hessian factors AA and BB, multiple options have been explored in the literature (see Section 5 and Section 6).

  2. 2.

    The information-theoretic view and waterfilling formula analyzed by Ordentlich and Polyanskiy (2026) and demonstrated experimentally by Lifar et al. (2026). Standard GPTQ allocates the same number of bits for every entry of VV. An alternative is to use entropy coding (Chen et al., 2026b; Lifar et al., 2026) for the quantized matrix. This allows in particular to ask about precision/bit/rate allocation: We have the freedom to store some entries in “higher precision” (usually costing more bits), and other entries with “lower precision” (using fewer bits). Concretely, “precision” corresponds to the scaling factors of the quantization grid. For example, Huffman-GPTQ (Chen et al., 2026b), which does use Huffman coding and thus encodes some entries with more bits and others with fewer, still distributes the precision/rate uniformly across all entries. If the variance Var⁡(xj)\mathrm{Var}(x_{j}) of the jjth input channel is known, a more effective way to distribute precision would be to assign to the jjth column of WW a scale proportional to 1/Var⁡(xj)1/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(x_{j})}. However, Ordentlich and Polyanskiy (2026); Lifar et al. (2026) notice that even that is suboptimal: In GPTQ, we can exploit linear correlation between different input channels, and what matters is only the residual variance that remains after accounting for this correlation. So the scale for the jjth column should be chosen proportional to 1/minej+1,…,en⁡Var⁡(xj−ej+1​xj+1−⋯−en​xn)1/\sqrt{\min_{e_{j+1},\dots,e_{n}}\mathrm{Var}(x_{j}-e_{j+1}x_{j+1}-\dots-e_{n}x_{n})}, and this is essentially optimal.

In this paper we use the information theoretic lens on the two-sided algorithm. First, this yields WaterKron, an extension of the existing waterfilling allocation, WaterSIC, to the Kronecker-factored geometry. Then we characterize its distortion in the full Hessian geometry, identify the penalty caused by the Kronecker approximation, and use it to find the optimal choice of Kronecker approximation. Concretely, we make the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    WaterKron: two-sided precision allocation. We extend the high-rate waterfilling results to two-sided GPTQ, deriving optimal row and column scales for the analyzed scalar-grid alphabet. Under the Gaussian and entropy-coding assumptions, this retains the approximately 0.250.25-bit asymptotic gap to the information-theoretic limit for the Kronecker distortion (Corollary 3.2). We demonstrate empirically that this outperforms allocating the waterfilling precision using only the input-sided Hessian (WaterSIC).

  2. 2.

    Quantifying the cost of Hessian mismatch. We characterize WaterKron’s high-rate distortion in the full Hessian geometry under the same assumptions. We introduce a mismatch factor Φ\Phi that quantifies the multiplicative distortion penalty caused by the Kronecker approximation, providing a criterion for choosing its factors (Theorem 4.1).

  3. 3.

    The FlipFlop Hessian. Minimizing the mismatch factor, we recover the flip-flop algorithm from Gaussian covariance fitting. We propose the resulting FlipFlop Hessian approximation, which is justified by its distortion-minimizing objective, and to the best of our knowledge has not been explored in this line of quantization research (Section 5). We demonstrate empirically that it outperforms previous choices of Hessian approximations from the quantization literature.

Our results extend the high-rate waterfilling theory of Ordentlich and Polyanskiy (2026); Lifar et al. (2026) to Kronecker-factored quadratic losses. It recovers (and improves), as a special case, the row- and column-dependent grid allocation of SoftWater (Cavalcanti and Wilson, 2026) which is designed for the Softmax module with a diagonal approximation of the output curvature BB.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. In Section 2 we recall the setting and previous work: standard GPTQ, its two-sided extension, and the waterfilling precision allocation. In Section 3 we first derive the optimal precision allocation for the two-sided algorithm. In Section 4 we take an information-theoretic viewpoint on the optimal choice of the Kronecker-factored Hessian approximation. We introduce the Kronecker-Hessian mismatch factor Φ\Phi and provide a variant of the rate-distortion result that takes the full Hessian into account. In Section 5, informed by the mismatch theory, we derive the ideal Kronecker approximation, proposing the FlipFlop Hessian. Lastly, we provide empirical evidence for the success of our methods in Section 6.

2 Setting and Background

In this section, we first describe the alphabet that is used for the remainder of the paper. Then we recall the standard GPTQ algorithm, its two-sided extension, and the waterfilling precision allocation.

Notation. For an mm by nn matrix MM, vec⁡(M)∈ℝm​n\vecop(M)\in\mathbb{R}^{mn} is its column-major vectorization. Assuming m=nm=n, we abbreviate |M|:=detM|M|:=\det M. If MM is additionally positive definite, Cholesky⁡(M)\mathrm{Cholesky}(M) denotes the unique lower-triangular matrix LL with positive diagonal entries Li,i>0L_{i,i}>0 that satisfies L​LT=MLL^{T}=M. Similarly, RevCholesky⁡(M)\mathrm{RevCholesky}(M) denotes the unique such LL that satisfies LT​L=ML^{T}L=M. Lastly, {0,1}∗=⋃n=0∞{0,1}n\{0,1\}^{*}=\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}\{0,1\}^{n} is the set of binary strings of arbitrary (but finite) length.

2.1 Alphabet

Recall that the goal of weight-only post-training quantization is to approximate W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with a matrix VV that has lower precision. For this paper, VV has the following structure:

  • •

    At its core, VV has essentially integer entries. We denote this integral matrix by Z∈ℤm×nZ\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}. The integers are unbounded (not clipped), and later encoded with a good coding scheme. Thus the memory cost of ZZ is determined by the entropy of the distribution of its entries.

  • •

    Additionally, there are real-valued scaling factors per row and per column. Concretely, the jjth column of VV is scaled by αj∈ℝ>0\alpha_{j}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and the iith row of VV is scaled by βi∈ℝ>0\beta_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}. These input/output scaling factor vectors α=(α1,…,αn)∈ℝn\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and β=(β1,…,βm)∈ℝm\beta=(\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{m} are stored in high precision. Their memory cost is very small.

So VV is an integer matrix ZZ whose rows and columns have been rescaled by β\beta and α\alpha. Concretely, the scaling factors form a rank-1 matrix β​αT∈ℝm×n\beta\alpha^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, and we have:

V=β​αT⊙ZVi,j=αj​βi⋅Zi,jV=\beta\alpha^{T}\odot Z\qquad\qquad V_{i,j}=\alpha_{j}\beta_{i}\cdot Z_{i,j}

Most importantly, the scaling factors can be used for distributing precision/rate across rows and columns. A small scaling factor corresponds to a high rate. For example, if α1\alpha_{1} is chosen to be very small, that means the scaled integer grid of column 1 is very fine-grained, so column 1 is stored in relatively high precision.

For the remainder of the paper, in particular in the algorithms, we will use Vi,jV_{i,j} as a variable that is implicitly defined as soon as Zi,jZ_{i,j}, αj\alpha_{j}, and βi\beta_{i} are defined/set/computed.

2.2 GPTQ: Adaptive Rounding

We recall the standard GPTQ algorithm by Frantar et al. (2023), described in Algorithm 1. The idea of this algorithm is to exploit the correlation between the nn input channels of the linear module W∈ℝm×nW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. The expected quadratic distortion can be expressed in several ways:

DA=1m​n​𝔼​∥V​x−W​x∥22=1m​n​∥(V−W)⋅𝔼​[x​xT]1/2∥F2=1m​n​∥(V−W)​LT∥F2D_{A}=\frac{1}{mn}\mathbb{E}\lVert Vx-Wx\rVert_{2}^{2}=\frac{1}{mn}\lVert(V-W)\cdot\mathbb{E}[xx^{T}]^{1/2}\rVert_{F}^{2}=\frac{1}{mn}\lVert(V-W)L^{T}\rVert_{F}^{2} (1)

Here x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is an input to the linear module WW. The expectation here, and in Section 5, is taken over an (empirical) calibration data distribution. M1/2M^{1/2} denotes an arbitrary matrix SS satisfying S​ST=MSS^{T}=M. In particular, one important choice for 𝔼​[x​xT]1/2\mathbb{E}[xx^{T}]^{1/2} is LTL^{T}, where L=RevCholesky⁡(𝔼⁡[x​xT])L=\mathrm{RevCholesky}(\mathbb{E}[xx^{T}]).11 1 If 𝔼⁡[x​xT]\mathbb{E}[xx^{T}] is not positive definite, a small damping κ​In\kappa I_{n} is added to it. This (reverse) Cholesky decomposition encodes linear correlation between the input channels, and sits at the heart of the GPTQ algorithm. This is because the core idea of the algorithm is to quantize the input channels sequentially, and modify WW along the way in order to partially correct the quantization error introduced by quantizing earlier input channels, which is only possible due to the correlation between those channels. See Algorithm 1.

2.3 Two-sided Extension and Kronecker-Factored Hessians

Later (Kim et al., 2025; Tseng et al., 2026; Birnick and Saab, 2026) it was realized that GPTQ can be naturally extended to also take the output geometry into account. Indeed, the Hessian of the minimization problem 𝔼​∥V​x−W​x∥22\mathbb{E}\lVert Vx-Wx\rVert_{2}^{2} with respect to v=vec⁡(V)v=\vecop(V) is (proportional to) 𝔼⁡[x​xT]⊗Im\mathbb{E}[xx^{T}]\otimes I_{m}. While the 𝔼⁡[x​xT]\mathbb{E}[xx^{T}] factor represents the input correlations that GPTQ exploits, the ImI_{m} factor means that all output channels are treated equally. The two-sided version of the algorithm instead considers an arbitrary Kronecker-factored Hessian A⊗BA\otimes B, which corresponds to the following two-sided distortion:

DA,B\displaystyle D_{A,B} =1m​n​∥(B1/2)T⋅(V−W)⋅A1/2∥F2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{mn}\lVert(B^{1/2})^{T}\cdot(V-W)\cdot A^{1/2}\rVert_{F}^{2} =1m​n​∥(vec⁡(V)T−vec⁡(W)T)⋅(A1/2⊗B1/2)∥F2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{mn}\lVert(\vecop(V)^{T}-\vecop(W)^{T})\cdot(A^{1/2}\otimes B^{1/2})\rVert_{F}^{2}
=1m​n​∥L(B)​(V−W)​(L(A))T∥F2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{mn}\lVert L^{(B)}(V-W)(L^{(A)})^{T}\rVert_{F}^{2} =1m​n​∥(vec⁡(V)T−vec⁡(W)T)​(L(A)⊗L(B))T∥F2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{mn}\lVert(\vecop(V)^{T}-\vecop(W)^{T})(L^{(A)}\otimes L^{(B)})^{T}\rVert_{F}^{2}

Here L(A)L^{(A)} is the reverse Cholesky decomposition of AA, and L(B)L^{(B)} is the reverse Cholesky decomposition of BB, and since matrix products distribute over Kronecker factors, L(A)⊗L(B)L^{(A)}\otimes L^{(B)} is the reverse Cholesky decomposition of A⊗BA\otimes B.

The identities from the right column, when compared to Equation 1, already reveal how the natural extension of GPTQ to a two-sided geometry works: We can just call Algorithm 1 with vec⁡(W)T∈ℝ1×m​n\vecop(W)^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times mn} as the weight matrix and A⊗B∈ℝm​n×m​nA\otimes B\in\mathbb{R}^{mn\times mn} as the input correlation matrix. This is described in Algorithm 2 in “unvectorized” notation. Note that if B=ImB=I_{m}, this is equivalent to Algorithm 1. For fast implementations of Algorithm 2 see Birnick and Saab (2026); Chen et al. (2026a).

2.4 Information Theoretic View and Waterfilling Formula

Note that GPTQ (Algorithm 1) and its two-sided extension (Algorithm 2) are at their core just about error propagation using the (reverse) Cholesky factors LL, and essentially independent of the alphabet that is used to store the entries. In particular, they do not postulate specific scaling factors α,β\alpha,\beta. Instead, those scaling factors are chosen up front and handed to the algorithm. For example, Huffman-GPTQ (Chen et al., 2026b) implicitly chooses α∝(1,…,1)\alpha\propto(1,\dots,1) and β∝(1,…,1)\beta\propto(1,\dots,1), i.e. a single scalar scaling factor for the whole matrix.

As noted in Section 2.1, the scaling factors can be used to distribute precision/rate across rows and columns non-uniformly. Ordentlich and Polyanskiy (2026) realized this and derived information-theoretically optimal scaling factors in the case of standard (only input-sided) GPTQ, i.e. Algorithm 1. Recall that in this setting we have

A=𝔼⁡[x​xT]L=RevCholesky⁡(A)L~=L−1=Cholesky⁡(A−1)A=\mathbb{E}[xx^{T}]\qquad L=\mathrm{RevCholesky}(A)\qquad\tilde{L}=L^{-1}=\mathrm{Cholesky}(A^{-1})

where the expectation is over calibration data. Ordentlich and Polyanskiy (2026); Lifar et al. (2026) then postulate the input scaling factor choice αj∝1/Lj,j=L~j,j\alpha_{j}\propto 1/L_{j,j}=\tilde{L}_{j,j}. Since they only consider the standard input-sided algorithm, they implicitly choose uniform output scaling factors β∝(1,…,1)\beta\propto(1,\dots,1).

They prove that, if Wi,j∼𝒩⁡(0,σW2)W_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{W}^{2}) is modeled as iid Gaussian, then Algorithm 1 with this choice of scaling factors is an (almost) information theoretically optimal quantization scheme for the distortion Equation 1. Concretely, they consider arbitrary encoder-decoder pairs: The encoder f:ℝm×n×ℝn×n→{0,1}∗f:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\to\{0,1\}^{*} takes (W,A)(W,A) and produces a self-delimiting (prefix-free) binary string, and the decoder g:{0,1}∗→ℝm×ng:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} takes the string and produces VV, so that we have V=g⁡(f⁡(W,A))V=g(f(W,A)). For example, one such encoder-decoder pair is given by Algorithm 1 together with an entropy coding scheme to encode/decode ZZ. (Here we gloss over encoding of α,β\alpha,\beta, see Section A.1.) For such a pair, the distortion DAD_{A} is measured as the expected input-sided distortion from Equation 1 and the rate RR as the expected string length per entry.

DA=1m​n​𝔼W​[∥(V−W)⋅A1/2∥F2]R=1m​n​𝔼W​[length⁡(f⁡(W,A))]D_{A}=\frac{1}{mn}\mathbb{E}_{W}\Big[\lVert(V-W)\cdot A^{1/2}\rVert_{F}^{2}\Big]\qquad R=\frac{1}{mn}\mathbb{E}_{W}\Big[\mathrm{length}(f(W,A))\Big] (2)

Note that at this point AA is seen as a deterministic Gram matrix, and the expectation runs over the Gaussian distribution of WW. In this setting, they prove the following theorems (reformulated).

Theorem 2.1 (IT lower bound).

Suppose that Wi,j∼𝒩⁡(0,σW2)W_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{W}^{2}) is iid Gaussian and A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is positive definite. Then any encoder-decoder pair (f,g)(f,g) satisfies:

DA≥σW2​|A|1/n​2−2​RD_{A}\geq\sigma_{W}^{2}|A|^{1/n}2^{-2R}
Theorem 2.2.

Suppose that Wi,j∼𝒩⁡(0,σW2)W_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{W}^{2}) is iid Gaussian and A∈ℝn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is positive definite. Additionally fix an entropy coding scheme that encodes ZZ with expected length H⁡(Z)+o⁡(m​n)H(Z)+o(mn). Then Algorithm 1 with scale choice αj=γ⋅|A|1/2​n/Lj,j\alpha_{j}=\gamma\cdot|A|^{1/2n}/L_{j,j} and βi=1\beta_{i}=1 achieves

DA=γ212​|A|1/n⋅(1+o⁡(1))R=12​log⁡(2​π​e​σW2)−log⁡γ+o⁡(1)D_{A}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{12}|A|^{1/n}\cdot(1+o(1))\qquad\qquad R=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma_{W}^{2})-\log\gamma+o(1)

as γ→0\gamma\to 0 and m​n→∞mn\to\infty. This yields the rate-distortion tradeoff

DA=2​π​e12⋅σW2​|A|1/n​2−2​R⋅(1+o⁡(1))D_{A}=\frac{2\pi e}{12}\cdot\sigma_{W}^{2}|A|^{1/n}2^{-2R}\cdot(1+o(1))

which, in the limit, is within 12​log⁡(2​π​e/12)≈0.255\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e/12)\approx 0.255 bits of the limiting rate from Theorem 2.1.

The scaling factor choice αj∝1/Lj,j\alpha_{j}\propto 1/L_{j,j} is known as the high-rate waterfilling rule. Algorithm 1 with these scaling factors, and potentially with other GPTQ improvements on top, is called the “WaterSIC” algorithm, see Lifar et al. (2026).

We will provide some intuition why αj∝1/Lj,j\alpha_{j}\propto 1/L_{j,j} is the correct choice of scaling factors, as this will become important in Section 5. For this, we will use that GPTQ is equivalent to Babai’s nearest plane algorithm (Babai, 1986) and take a lattice perspective (Birnick, 2026; Chen et al., 2026b). Algorithm 1 is equivalent to running Babai’s algorithm on the lattice L​diag​(α)​ℤnL\mathrm{diag}(\alpha)\mathbb{Z}^{n} with target vectors LWi,:TLW_{i,:}^{T}. It tiles the plane into copies of a rectangular fundamental region, where the rectangle has side lengths (α1​L1,1,…,αn​Ln,n)(\alpha_{1}L_{1,1},\dots,\alpha_{n}L_{n,n}). Each target vector is quantized to the lattice vector at the center of the rectangle that it lies inside. Denote the rectangle around the zero vector by E=∏j=1n[−αjLj,j/2,αjLj,j/2]E=\prod_{j=1}^{n}[-\alpha_{j}L_{j,j}/2,\alpha_{j}L_{j,j}/2]. The quantization error vectors L(Vi,:−Wi,:)TL(V_{i,:}-W_{i,:})^{T} lie in this region. In the high rate regime (where the scaling factors approach zero), the error vectors are approximately uniformly distributed within EE. Thus the distortion is:

DA=1n𝔼W,i[∥(Vi,:−Wi,:)LT∥F2]≈1n𝔼e∼Unif⁡(E)[∥e∥22]=1121n∑j=1n(αjLj,j)2D_{A}=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}_{W,i}\Big[\lVert(V_{i,:}-W_{i,:})L^{T}\rVert_{F}^{2}\Big]\approx\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}_{e\sim\mathrm{Unif}(E)}\Big[\lVert e\rVert_{2}^{2}\Big]=\frac{1}{12}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(\alpha_{j}L_{j,j})^{2} (3)

Moreover, fixing the rate RR corresponds to fixing the volume of the rectangle EE. So minimizing distortion at a given rate corresponds to minimizing Equation 3 while leaving Vol⁡(E)=∏j=1nαj​Lj,j\mathrm{Vol}(E)=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{j}L_{j,j} fixed. This is achieved by making the side lengths of EE all equal, so that it becomes a cube. This yields αj∝1/Lj,j\alpha_{j}\propto 1/L_{j,j}. See Figure 1 for a visualization.

3 Two-sided Rate Allocation

We aim to unify the two-sided Algorithm 2 from Section 2.3 with the information theoretic view on Algorithm 1 from Section 2.4. The first step is to choose the scaling factors α\alpha and β\beta for Algorithm 2 appropriately. Perhaps unsurprisingly, we show that the optimal choice is αj∝1/Lj,j(A)\alpha_{j}\propto 1/L^{(A)}_{j,j} and βi∝1/Li,i(B)\beta_{i}\propto 1/L^{(B)}_{i,i}. This follows directly from viewing Algorithm 2 as being equivalent to Algorithm 1 on a transformed input. We establish the corresponding information theoretic and achievability theorems for the two-sided Algorithm 2.

Concretely, let Wi,j∼𝒩⁡(0,σW2)W_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{W}^{2}) iid Gaussian, let the encoder f:ℝm×n×ℝn×n×ℝm×m→{0,1}∗f:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\times\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\to\{0,1\}^{*} take (W,A,B)(W,A,B), let the decoder g:{0,1}∗→ℝm×ng:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be as before, and define rate and distortion in the two-sided setting as follows:

DA,B=1m​n​𝔼W​[∥(B1/2)T​(V−W)⋅A1/2∥F2]R=1m​n​𝔼W​[length⁡(f⁡(W,A,B))]D_{A,B}=\frac{1}{mn}\mathbb{E}_{W}\Big[\lVert(B^{1/2})^{T}(V-W)\cdot A^{1/2}\rVert_{F}^{2}\Big]\qquad R=\frac{1}{mn}\mathbb{E}_{W}\Big[\mathrm{length}(f(W,A,B))\Big] (4)

Then we have the following results as the two-sided versions of Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.2.

Corollary 3.1 (IT lower bound).

Suppose that Wi,j∼𝒩⁡(0,σW2)W_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{W}^{2}) is iid Gaussian and A,BA,B are positive definite. Then any encoder-decoder pair (f,g)(f,g) satisfies:

DA,B≥σW2​|A|1/n​|B|1/m​2−2​RD_{A,B}\geq\sigma_{W}^{2}|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}2^{-2R}
Proof.

Define n^:=m​n\hat{n}:=mn and m^:=1\hat{m}:=1, as well as A^:=A⊗B∈ℝn^×n^\hat{A}:=A\otimes B\in\mathbb{R}^{\hat{n}\times\hat{n}} and W^:=vec⁡(W)T∈ℝm^×n^\hat{W}:=\vecop(W)^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{\hat{m}\times\hat{n}}. Then note that iid W^i,j∼𝒩⁡(0,σW2)\hat{W}_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{W}^{2}) and invoke Theorem 2.1 with W^\hat{W} and A^\hat{A} . Lastly, note that the rate and distortion definitions 2 applied for A^,W^\hat{A},\hat{W} transform exactly to the rate and distortion definitions 4 for A,B,WA,B,W, e.g. DA,B=DA^D_{A,B}=D_{\hat{A}}, and that |A^|1/n^=|A⊗B|1/(m​n)=(|A|m​|B|n)1/(m​n)=|A|1/n​|B|1/m|\hat{A}|^{1/\hat{n}}=|A\otimes B|^{1/(mn)}=(|A|^{m}|B|^{n})^{1/(mn)}=|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}. So the conclusion of our invocation of Theorem 2.1 is exactly the conclusion of this theorem. ∎

Corollary 3.2.

Suppose that Wi,j∼𝒩⁡(0,σW2)W_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{W}^{2}) is iid Gaussian and A,BA,B are positive definite. Additionally fix an entropy coding scheme that encodes ZZ with expected length H⁡(Z)+o⁡(m​n)H(Z)+o(mn). Then Algorithm 2 with scale choice αj=γ⋅|A|1/2​n/Lj,j(A)\alpha_{j}=\sqrt{\gamma}\cdot|A|^{1/2n}/L^{(A)}_{j,j} and βi=γ⋅|B|1/2​m/Li,i(B)\beta_{i}=\sqrt{\gamma}\cdot|B|^{1/2m}/L^{(B)}_{i,i} achieves

DA,B=γ212​|A|1/n​|B|1/m⋅(1+o⁡(1))R=12​log⁡(2​π​e​σW2)−log⁡γ+o⁡(1)D_{A,B}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{12}|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}\cdot(1+o(1))\qquad\qquad R=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma_{W}^{2})-\log\gamma+o(1)

as γ→0\gamma\to 0 and m​n→∞mn\to\infty. This yields the rate-distortion tradeoff

DA,B=2​π​e12⋅σW2​|A|1/n​|B|1/m​2−2​R⋅(1+o⁡(1))D_{A,B}=\frac{2\pi e}{12}\cdot\sigma_{W}^{2}|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}2^{-2R}\cdot(1+o(1))

which, in the limit, is within 12​log⁡(2​π​e/12)≈0.25\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e/12)\approx 0.25 bits of the limiting rate from Corollary 3.1.

Proof.

We again define n^:=m​n\hat{n}:=mn and m^:=1\hat{m}:=1, then A^:=A⊗B∈ℝn^×n^\hat{A}:=A\otimes B\in\mathbb{R}^{\hat{n}\times\hat{n}} and W^:=vec⁡(W)T∈ℝm^×n^\hat{W}:=\vecop(W)^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{\hat{m}\times\hat{n}}, and also α^=α⊗β∈ℝn^\hat{\alpha}=\alpha\otimes\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{\hat{n}} and β^=1∈ℝm^\hat{\beta}=1\in\mathbb{R}^{\hat{m}}. Define L^,L(A),L(B)\hat{L},L^{(A)},L^{(B)} as the reverse Cholesky decompositions of A^,A,B\hat{A},A,B, and note that L^=L(A)⊗L(B)\hat{L}=L^{(A)}\otimes L^{(B)}. Here, again, we have iid W^i,j∼𝒩⁡(0,σW2)\hat{W}_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{W}^{2}) and we invoke Theorem 2.2 with W^\hat{W} and A^\hat{A}.

Now note that calling Algorithm 1 with W^,A^,α^,β^\hat{W},\hat{A},\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta}, upon unvectorizing the resulting V^\hat{V} (or Z^\hat{Z}) back into an mm by nn matrix, is equivalent to calling Algorithm 2 with W,A,B,α,βW,A,B,\alpha,\beta. And if, for any pair (i,j)(i,j), we define j^:=(j−1)​m+i\hat{j}:=(j-1)m+i, then we have

α^j^=(α⊗β)j^=αj​βi=γ⋅|A|1/2​n/Lj,j(A)⋅γ⋅|B|1/2​m/Li,i(B)=γ⋅|A^|1/2​n^/L^j^,j^\hat{\alpha}_{\hat{j}}=(\alpha\otimes\beta)_{\hat{j}}=\alpha_{j}\beta_{i}=\sqrt{\gamma}\cdot|A|^{1/2n}/L^{(A)}_{j,j}\cdot\sqrt{\gamma}\cdot|B|^{1/2m}/L^{(B)}_{i,i}=\gamma\cdot|\hat{A}|^{1/2\hat{n}}/\hat{L}_{\hat{j},\hat{j}}

which shows that the scaling factors prescribed by this theorem indeed correspond to the scaling factors prescribed by our invocation of Theorem 2.2. Again, the rate and distortion definitions from 2 and 4 match too, DA,B=DA^D_{A,B}=D_{\hat{A}}, and so the conclusion of our invocation of Theorem 2.2 is exactly the conclusion of this theorem. ∎

Remark.

There is only one subtlety to be careful about, and that is the entropy coding scheme for ZZ. For the algorithm from Theorem 2.2, Lifar et al. (2026) suggest to use Huffman coding for every column, which is possible since all the entries in one column jj have the same scaling factor αj\alpha_{j}, due to the row scaling factors β=(1,…,1)\beta=(1,\dots,1) being trivial. For the algorithm in this theorem, this kind of Huffman coding is no longer efficient enough since both α\alpha and β\beta are nontrivial, and thus every entry (i,j)(i,j) has a unique scaling factor αj​βi\alpha_{j}\beta_{i}. However, there are other entropy coding schemes that can deal with this, such as variants of arithmetic coding.

4 Kronecker-Hessian Mismatch Factor

For the two-sided algorithm, we have so far analyzed it with the distortion measure DA,BD_{A,B}, which implicitly assumes a Kronecker-factored Hessian structure A⊗BA\otimes B. However, in reality, the Kronecker product A⊗BA\otimes B is only an approximation to some “full Hessian” H∈ℝm​n×m​nH\in\mathbb{R}^{mn\times mn} that truly captures the geometry of the problem, but is too big to directly deal with algorithmically. In practice, HH is usually the Fisher information matrix of WW, see Section 5. The true distortion must be measured with respect to HH, which leads to the following distortion measure:

DH=1m​n​𝔼W​[∥(vec⁡(V)T−vec⁡(W)T)⋅H1/2∥F2]D_{H}=\frac{1}{mn}\mathbb{E}_{W}\Big[\lVert(\vecop(V)^{T}-\vecop(W)^{T})\cdot H^{1/2}\rVert_{F}^{2}\Big] (5)

We now show that when approximating HH by A⊗BA\otimes B and running Algorithm 2 with A,BA,B, then the full distortion DHD_{H} is asymptotically equal to the two-sided distortion DA,BD_{A,B} from Corollary 3.2 times tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)/m​n\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})/mn.

Note that it is not generally true that DH=DA,B⋅tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)/m​nD_{H}=D_{A,B}\cdot\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})/mn. In general there is a correction term, which for Algorithm 2 in the setting of our theorem becomes negligible as the quantization errors in EE become asymptotically uniformly distributed.

Theorem 4.1.

Suppose that Wi,j∼𝒩⁡(0,σW2)W_{i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{W}^{2}) is iid Gaussian and H,A,BH,A,B are positive definite. Additionally fix an entropy coding scheme that encodes ZZ with expected length H⁡(Z)+o⁡(m​n)H(Z)+o(mn). Then Algorithm 2 with scale choice αj=γ⋅|A|1/2​n/Lj,j(A)\alpha_{j}=\sqrt{\gamma}\cdot|A|^{1/2n}/L^{(A)}_{j,j} and βi=γ⋅|B|1/2​m/Li,i(B)\beta_{i}=\sqrt{\gamma}\cdot|B|^{1/2m}/L^{(B)}_{i,i} achieves

DH=γ212​|A|1/n​|B|1/m​tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)m​n⋅(1+o⁡(1))R=12​log⁡(2​π​e​σW2)−log⁡γ+o⁡(1)D_{H}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{12}|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}\frac{\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})}{mn}\cdot(1+o(1))\qquad R=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma_{W}^{2})-\log\gamma+o(1)

as γ→0\gamma\to 0 and m​n→∞mn\to\infty. This yields the rate-distortion tradeoff:

DH=2​π​e12⋅σW2​|A|1/n​|B|1/m​tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)m​n​2−2​R⋅(1+o⁡(1))D_{H}=\frac{2\pi e}{12}\cdot\sigma_{W}^{2}|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}\frac{\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})}{mn}2^{-2R}\cdot(1+o(1))
Proof.

The setting is the same as in Corollary 3.2, which also already provides us with the rate R=12​log⁡(2​π​e​σW2)−log⁡γ+o⁡(1)R=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma_{W}^{2})-\log\gamma+o(1). We only have to compute the distortion DHD_{H} with respect to the full Hessian. To compute it, recall the intuition from Section 2.4. For the two-sided algorithm, the “error region” in the lattice space is

E:=∏j=1n∏i=1m[−αjβiLj,j(A)Li,i(B)/2,αjβiLj,j(A)Li,i(B)/2]E:=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\prod_{i=1}^{m}[-\alpha_{j}\beta_{i}L^{(A)}_{j,j}L^{(B)}_{i,i}/2,\alpha_{j}\beta_{i}L^{(A)}_{j,j}L^{(B)}_{i,i}/2]

The scaling factors are chosen exactly so that this becomes a cube. Concretely, we have:

E=|A|1/2​n|B|1/2​m⋅∏j=1n∏i=1m[−γ/2,γ/2]E=|A|^{1/2n}|B|^{1/2m}\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{n}\prod_{i=1}^{m}[-\gamma/2,\gamma/2]

The transformed quantization error vec⁡(L(B)​(V−W)​(L(A))T)\vecop(L^{(B)}(V-W)(L^{(A)})^{T}) lies in EE. We make the simplifying assumption to work only in the high-rate limit γ→0\gamma\to 0 and assume that this transformed quantization error vector is uniformly distributed in EE. As γ→0\gamma\to 0 this holds asymptotically because WW is normally distributed; intuitively, in Figure 1, the rectangles/cubes become so small that the blue dots become approximately uniformly distributed within them. For a concrete proof of this, see Lifar et al. (2026, Appendix B.2). Write L:=L(A)⊗L(B)L:=L^{(A)}\otimes L^{(B)}, d:=vec⁡(V−W)d:=\vecop(V-W), and note that e:=L​de:=Ld is the transformed quantization error vec⁡(L(B)​(V−W)​(L(A))T)∈E\vecop(L^{(B)}(V-W)(L^{(A)})^{T})\in E. So d:=L−1​ed:=L^{-1}e where ee is asymptotically uniformly distributed, giving:

DH\displaystyle D_{H} =1m​n​𝔼W​[dT​H​d]=1m​n​𝔼W​[tr⁡(H​d​dT)]=1m​n​𝔼W​[tr⁡(H​L−1​e​eT​L−T)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{mn}\mathbb{E}_{W}[d^{T}Hd]=\frac{1}{mn}\mathbb{E}_{W}[\tr(Hdd^{T})]=\frac{1}{mn}\mathbb{E}_{W}[\tr(HL^{-1}ee^{T}L^{-T})]
≍γ→0​1m​n​tr⁡(H​L−1​𝔼e∼Unif⁡(E)​[e​eT]​L−T)=1m​n​|A|1/n​|B|1/m​γ212​tr⁡(H​L−1​I​L−T)\displaystyle\overset{\mathclap{\gamma\to 0}}{\asymp}\frac{1}{mn}\tr(HL^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{e\sim\mathrm{Unif}(E)}[ee^{T}]L^{-T})=\frac{1}{mn}\frac{|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}\gamma^{2}}{12}\tr(HL^{-1}IL^{-T})
=γ212​|A|1/n​|B|1/m​tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)m​n\displaystyle=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{12}|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}\frac{\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})}{mn}

∎

Theorem 4.1 now gives us a clear path on how to choose the Hessian approximation A⊗BA\otimes B in order to minimize distortion: We have to minimize the term in the distortion that depends on A,BA,B, which is |A|1/n​|B|1/m⋅tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)m​n|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}\cdot\frac{\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})}{mn}. It is cleanest to additionally normalize this by |H|1/m​n|H|^{1/mn}. We call the resulting metric the Kronecker-Hessian mismatch factor and abbreviate it as Φ\Phi:

Φ⁡(H,A⊗B):=tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)/m​n|H|1/m​n⋅|A|−1/n|B|−1/m=tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)/m​n|H|1/m​n⋅|A⊗B|−1/mn\Phi(H,A\otimes B):=\frac{\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})/mn}{|H|^{1/mn}\cdot|A|^{-1/n}|B|^{-1/m}}=\frac{\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})/mn}{|H|^{1/mn}\cdot|A\otimes B|^{-1/mn}}

The mismatch factor has the following additional interpretations. First, define the generalized eigenvalues λ1,…,λm​n\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{mn} of (H,A⊗B)(H,A\otimes B) as the eigenvalues of ((A⊗B)1/2)−1​H​((A⊗B)1/2)−T((A\otimes B)^{1/2})^{-1}H((A\otimes B)^{1/2})^{-T}. Then Φ\Phi is the ratio of the arithmetic mean and the geometric mean of those generalized eigenvalues:

Φ⁡(H,A⊗B)=1m​n​∑k=1m​nλk(∏k=1m​nλk)1/m​n=AM⁡(λ1,…,λm​n)GM⁡(λ1,…,λm​n)\Phi(H,A\otimes B)=\frac{\frac{1}{mn}\sum_{k=1}^{mn}\lambda_{k}}{(\prod_{k=1}^{mn}\lambda_{k})^{1/mn}}=\frac{\mathrm{AM}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{mn})}{\mathrm{GM}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{mn})}

Note that the AM–GM inequality gives Φ⁡(H,A⊗B)≥1\Phi(H,A\otimes B)\geq 1, with equality if and only if HH is a positive scalar multiple of A⊗BA\otimes B. In transform coding, this is also known as the coding gain, see Gersho and Gray (2012, chapter 8).

Second, up to scaling A⊗BA\otimes B by some s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, it is essentially equal to the exponential of the KL-divergence between Gaussians with covariance HH and A⊗BA\otimes B, respectively:

logΦ(H,A⊗B)=2m​nmins>0DKL(𝒩(0,H)∥𝒩(0,s⋅A⊗B))\log\Phi(H,A\otimes B)=\frac{2}{mn}\min_{s>0}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal{N}(0,H)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(0,s\cdot A\otimes B)) (6)

5 The FlipFlop Hessian Approximation

In order to minimize the distortion in Theorem 4.1, we have to find a Hessian approximation A⊗BA\otimes B of HH that minimizes Φ⁡(H,A⊗B)\Phi(H,A\otimes B). In general, this minimization problem has no closed form solution. But it turns out that there is an efficient algorithm that converges to the solution.

We work in the setting where HH can be written as an expectation over outer products of Kronecker-factored vectors:

H=𝔼x,g​[(x⊗g)​(x⊗g)T]=𝔼x,g​[x​xT⊗g​gT]H=\mathbb{E}_{x,g}[(x\otimes g)(x\otimes g)^{T}]=\mathbb{E}_{x,g}[xx^{T}\otimes gg^{T}]

Here x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and g∈ℝmg\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, and we will drop the subscript x,gx,g from the expectation for the remainder of the section. There is a very natural setting where this is the case, namely when HH is the Fisher information matrix of WW, or equivalently the Hessian of the cross entropy loss with respect to the network’s own predictive distribution. In that case, xx would be a calibration input of WW, y=W​xy=Wx, a network output is sampled from the model’s predictive distribution, and gg is the gradient of the negative log-likelihood of this network output with respect to yy (see for example Birnick and Saab (2026)).

We now wish to find A,BA,B that minimize Φ⁡(H,A⊗B)=tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)/m​n|H|1/m​n⋅|A|−1/n|B|−1/m\Phi(H,A\otimes B)=\frac{\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})/mn}{|H|^{1/mn}\cdot|A|^{-1/n}|B|^{-1/m}}. Write G:=g​xT∈ℝm×nG:=gx^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and note that vec⁡(G)=x⊗g\vecop(G)=x\otimes g. From trace and Kronecker identities we get:

tr⁡(H​(A⊗B)−1)=tr⁡(𝔼⁡[vec⁡(G)​vec⁡(G)T]​(A−1⊗B−1))=𝔼​tr⁡(B−1​G​A−1​GT)\tr(H(A\otimes B)^{-1})=\tr(\mathbb{E}[\vecop(G)\vecop(G)^{T}](A^{-1}\otimes B^{-1}))=\mathbb{E}\tr(B^{-1}GA^{-1}G^{T})

Thus we can rewrite the objective Φ\Phi, and also simplify it by removing constants:

Φ⁡(H,A⊗B)∝|A|1/n​|B|1/m⋅𝔼​tr⁡(B−1​G​A−1​GT)\Phi(H,A\otimes B)\quad\propto\quad|A|^{1/n}|B|^{1/m}\cdot\mathbb{E}\tr(B^{-1}GA^{-1}G^{T})

Now we fix AA, and ask for the best choice of BB given AA. The objective for BB is proportional to

|B|1/m⋅tr⁡(B−1​S)withS:=𝔼⁡[G​A−1​GT].|B|^{1/m}\cdot\tr(B^{-1}S)\quad\text{with}\quad S:=\mathbb{E}[GA^{-1}G^{T}].

This is minimized when BB is proportional to SS. Indeed, the AM-GM inequality applied to the eigenvalues of B−1​SB^{-1}S says tr⁡(B−1​S)/m≥(|S|/|B|)1/m\tr(B^{-1}S)/m\geq(|S|/|B|)^{1/m} and equality holds when the eigenvalues are all the same, leading to B∝SB\propto S. Similarly, when BB is fixed, then AA minimizes Φ\Phi precisely when A∝𝔼⁡[GT​B−1​G]A\propto\mathbb{E}[G^{T}B^{-1}G]. This naturally leads to the following alternating (fixed point) iteration:

Ak+1\displaystyle A_{k+1} ∝𝔼⁡[GT​Bk−1​G]=𝔼⁡[gT​Bk−1​g⋅x​xT]\displaystyle\propto\mathbb{E}[G^{T}B_{k}^{-1}G]=\mathbb{E}[g^{T}B_{k}^{-1}g\cdot xx^{T}]
Bk+1\displaystyle B_{k+1} ∝𝔼⁡[G​Ak+1−1​GT]=𝔼⁡[xT​Ak+1−1​x⋅g​gT]\displaystyle\propto\mathbb{E}[GA_{k+1}^{-1}G^{T}]=\mathbb{E}[x^{T}A_{k+1}^{-1}x\cdot gg^{T}]

In maximum likelihood estimation of matrix normal distributions, this is known as the “flip-flop algorithm” (Dutilleul, 1999). If HH is positive definite, then it converges to a unique (up to scaling) fixed point (Hoff et al., 2023, section 2). Indeed, the connection to Gaussian maximum likelihood estimation is given by Equation 6. For this reason, we call the resulting approximation A⊗BA\otimes B of HH the FlipFlop Hessian.

Interestingly, the algorithm resembles a power iteration that was previously explored for the two-sided GPTQ algorithm. Namely, if Ak+1−1A_{k+1}^{-1}, Bk−1B_{k}^{-1} above are replaced by Ak+1A_{k+1}, BkB_{k}, so that the weighting is in some sense reciprocal, then the algorithm can be interpreted as a power iteration that minimizes ∥H−A⊗B∥F\lVert H-A\otimes B\rVert_{F}, see Tseng et al. (2026); Birnick and Saab (2026). We call the resulting approximation the Frobenius Hessian. It can be interpreted as the best “additive” Kronecker approximation to HH, while the FlipFlop Hessian can be interpreted as the best “multiplicative” approximation in a certain sense. We demonstrate in Section 6 that the FlipFlop outperforms the Frobenius Hessian in practice, as suggested by the theory.

6 Experiments

Setup. We quantize and evaluate Llama (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Qwen (Yang et al., 2025) models with up to 4B parameters at a target entropy of 2 bits per weight. Calibration uses 256 sequences of 2048 tokens from Pile10k, a subset of The Pile (Gao et al., 2020). Inputs xx are always from the unquantized model, in contrast to using a x^\hat{x} that went through the partially-quantized model as usually done with GPTQ. The gradients are computed in an empirical Fisher fashion, meaning that labels are not sampled from the model’s predictive distribution but taken as next token from the calibration dataset. Hessians are damped with 0.10.1 times the mean diagonal for both factors, including between iterations of the flip-flop algorithm. The Hessian approximations that we compare are listed in Table 1. For Frobenius and FlipFlop approximations, which both use the alternating fixed point iteration, we additionally compare different numbers of iterations. AA is initialized as InI_{n}, and then one iteration corresponds to updating both BB and AA once. The number of iterations is appended as a suffix to the name, e.g. “FlipFlop-1”, “FlipFlop-2”, etc. We evaluate DKL(punquantized∥pquantized)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\mathrm{unquantized}}\|p_{\mathrm{quantized}}) (KL) and perplexity (PPL), on both the calibration dataset (Pile10k) and the WikiText-2 test split (Merity et al., 2016). See Tables 2, 3, 4 and 5 for the results. Lower is better and bold marks the best quantized result in each column.

Findings. We find that generally the two-sided (“WaterKron”) variants outperform the purely input-sided (“WaterSIC”) variant. The Frobenius variant (as used for example by YAQA (Tseng et al., 2026)) generally gets worse with more iterations (measured up to 3 iterations). For Qwen3-4B it even gets worse than the purely input-sided Hessian. This supports the argument against minimizing ∥H−A⊗B∥\lVert H-A\otimes B\rVert. Our new FlipFlop variant generally improves with the second iteration, and is consistently the best of all the variants, supporting the argument that Φ⁡(H,A⊗B)\Phi(H,A\otimes B) is a more appropriate metric to minimize. Interestingly, for Qwen models, three FlipFlop iterations are usually slightly worse than just two iterations.

Appendix A Technical Details

For the theorems in this paper there are two technicalities that we deliberately left without comment in order to focus on the core statements. In this section we will clarify these technicalities.

A.1 Encoding of the scaling factors α\alpha, β\beta

Theorem 2.2, Corollary 3.2, Theorem 4.1 only consider the encoding of Z∈ℤm×nZ\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n} and ignore the encoding of the scaling factors α∈ℝn\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{n} and β∈ℝm\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. This is to keep the theorem statement clean. In practice, the memory cost of the scaling factors is negligible. For the theoretical coding argument, we can give the decoder direct access to α,β\alpha,\beta, so there is no need to encode them. In fact, the decoder can even be given full access to AA,BB (which in particular recover α,β\alpha,\beta), as the lower bounds of Theorem 2.1, Corollary 3.1 still hold true even with this more powerful decoder.

Concretely, the decoder gg would then be a function g:({0,1}∗,ℝn×n,ℝm×m)→ℝm×ng:(\{0,1\}^{*},\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\mathbb{R}^{m\times m})\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, taking a string and AA, BB, and producing VV. For Algorithm 2, the string would be the entropy-coded ZZ, and α,β\alpha,\beta as defined in Corollary 3.2 can be found from A,BA,B, so the decoder can find V=β​αT⊙ZV=\beta\alpha^{T}\odot Z. Now, with this more powerful decoder, one could worry that the lower bound Corollary 3.1 would not hold anymore, as a decoder with access to A,BA,B perhaps allows for a much more efficient scheme; but this is not the case. Indeed, the standard proof of Corollary 3.1 already assumes decoder access to AA and BB, see Ordentlich and Polyanskiy (2026); Lifar et al. (2026).

A.2 Limit γ→0\gamma\to 0 and m​n→∞mn\to\infty

Theorem 2.2, Corollary 3.2, Theorem 4.1 all consider the limit γ→0\gamma\to 0 and m​n→∞mn\to\infty. The limit γ→0\gamma\to 0 makes sure that we are in the high rate regime where the transformed quantization errors become uniformly distributed. The limit m​n→∞mn\to\infty, i.e. growing matrix size, is to ensure the efficiency of the coding scheme, so that it can approach the entropy of the distribution of ZZ. Note that due to the second limit, these theorems are technically not about a fixed A,BA,B, but about all of them at the same time. In this case, one needs to be careful how the joint limit γ→0\gamma\to 0 and m​n→∞mn\to\infty is taken. We understand it in an iterated sense: First take γ→0\gamma\to 0 for fixed A,BA,B, then take m​n→∞mn\to\infty. Then for each concrete instance of A,BA,B it is ensured that we are in the high-rate limit where the transformed quantization errors are uniformly distributed.
